output.question: What lawsuits is DoorDash involved in?
output.answer: As of November 2026, sources describe several DoorDash legal matters. The most recent one I found is a Pennsylvania (Luzerne County) injury suit against Uber Eats and DoorDash over a 2023 crash, which reportedly settled confidentially on October 28, 2026, three weeks into trial. A Palm Beach County suit filed October 8 alleges a driver assaulted a customer after an alcohol delivery. The largest recent resolution is a $131.5 million settlement with New York City's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) over underpaid and late courier pay, announced September 22, 2026. That was a city enforcement action, not a class action. Still pending, according to secondary sources: a Seattle suit over Dasher deactivations (Slawson et al. v. DoorDash, King County Superior Court, filed June 15, 2026), a proposed DashPass 'junk fee' class action filed April 15, 2026 in San Francisco Superior Court, and continuing worker-classification matters. A federal data-breach suit (Andrizzi v. DoorDash, N.D. Cal.) appears on the docket as terminated on April 8, 2026, and a securities firm announced an investor investigation (not a filed suit) on October 19, 2026.

key_facts.fact: A Pennsylvania crash suit against Uber Eats and DoorDash (Luzerne County, Judge Richard M. Hughes III) ended in a confidential settlement on October 28, 2026, three weeks into a trial that began October 6. The records are sealed.
A Palm Beach County suit filed October 8 alleges a DoorDash driver assaulted a customer after an alcohol delivery.
A securities firm announced an investor investigation on October 19, 2026, after the stock fell more than 7.7%. This is an investigation, not a filed suit.

DoorDash agreed to a $131.5M settlement with NYC's DCWP over underpaid and late courier pay. The listed parts are $12.3M to couriers, about $83M to settle a dispute over pay for on-call time, and $16.7M in fines to DCWP.

Slawson et al. v. DoorDash Inc. (No. 26-2-19283-9, King County Superior Court), filed June 15, 2026, alleges DoorDash removed Seattle Dashers without the notice and process the city's deactivation ordinance requires. It is pending.

A proposed class action filed April 15, 2026 in San Francisco Superior Court alleges DashPass members promised $0 delivery were still charged a mandatory service fee. It seeks restitution and injunctive relief. No class has been certified.
The data-breach suit Andrizzi v. DoorDash Inc. (No. 3:25-cv-09926, N.D. Cal.), filed November 18, 2025, is listed in federal docket data as terminated on April 8, 2026. The reason is unconfirmed.
DoorDash's Q3 2026 10-Q, in its Deliveroo purchase price allocation, records $99 million of acquired contingent liabilities relating to outstanding legal provisions.

passages.quote: ended in a confidential settlement, three weeks into a trial that began October 6.
a Palm Beach County suit filed October 8 alleging a driver assaulted a customer after an alcohol delivery.
alleges DoorDash removed Seattle Dashers without the notice and process the city's deactivation ordinance requires.
federal docket data list the case as terminated on 2026-04-08, and we could not confirm why.
Acquired contingent liabilities relate to outstanding legal provisions

caveats: I couldn't read the Legal Proceedings section (Part II, Item 1) or the Commitments and Contingencies note of DoorDash's Q3 2026 10-Q because the SEC page cut off before them. So the company's own list of material matters (for example, worker-classification suits and attorney-general actions) is not verified here.
The details of the Pennsylvania, Palm Beach, Seattle, data-breach and investor-investigation matters come from a secondary legal-news site (settlementinsight.com), not court dockets.

The DashPass suit details come from a third-party news aggregator (rallies.ai). Plaintiffs aren't named, and the court is given only as 'California' there and as San Francisco Superior Court elsewhere.

The NYC $131.5M deal is a city enforcement settlement, not a class-action lawsuit. The three components NRN lists add up to about $112M, so the remaining roughly $19.5M is unaccounted for in that article.
Legal-SEO sites also mention a $16.75M fee or tip settlement, but they describe it inconsistently, so I left it out.
Some of these matters may have changed status since the sources were published.
